decisions.quote: Reassigning responsibility is the most prominent and best-replicated intervention against escalating commitment (i.e., the failure to withdraw from losing courses of action). This intervention is considered effective because it reduces reinvestments after negative feedback in decision scenarios with a single reinvestment decision. However, we argue that any intervention against escalating commitment should fulfill two additional criteria. The first is temporal stability, that is, the beneficial effects of the intervention need to persist beyond a single reinvestment decision. The second is specific effectiveness, that is, the intervention should reduce commitment only if the project continues to fail after an initial setback (structural failure) but not if it recovers and is ultimately profitable (temporary failure). To subject reassignment of responsibility to this critical test of effectiveness, we introduce a modification of the escalation paradigm that allows testing for temporal stability and differentiates between structural and temporary failure.
decisions.reason: The available source text (10.1037/xap0000366, Schultze & Schulz-Hardt, 2022) consists only of the title, authors, DOI, and abstract. The abstract states that the paper empirically retests the intervention of reassigning responsibility against escalating commitment across two experiments using a modified escalation paradigm. However, the abstract contains no citations, author names, publication years, titles, or DOIs for the original study or studies establishing the responsibility-reassignment intervention or escalation paradigm. Consequently, primary source evidence is insufficient to establish whether the retested original is already represented by shipped row 1509 (Staw, 1976, 'Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action', DOI 10.1016/0030-5073(76)90005-2) or whether an unshipped original paper is being retested.

decisions.quote:
Thus, we sought to replicate and extend prior work on 
the MDNM using a large, multisite sample of college men. Our study aims are to investigate 
the factor structure and item loadings of the MDNM, and examine the extent to which 
excess and control are associated with alcohol use and negative drinking consequences 
over and above known demographic correlates of alcohol use including age, membership 
in a Greek fraternity and/or athletic involvement (e.g., Meilman et al., 1999; Merrill & 
Carey, 2016; Zhou & Heim, 2014) and general masculine norms (CMNI-29). Based on prior 
research (Perrotte et al., 2020; Zamboanga et al., 2023), we expected to find a two-factor 
solution (i.e., excess and control) of the MDNM in this multisite sample of college men. 
We also expected excess to be positively associated with alcohol use and negative drinking 
consequences and control to be negatively related to both drinking outcomes.
decisions.reason: The primary source (Zamboanga et al., 2025, DOI 10.1037/men0000497) collects new multisite survey data (N = 1,350 college men across 12 universities) to empirically retest the two-factor structure (excess and control) of the Masculine Drinking Norms Measure (MDNM) and its multivariate associations with alcohol use (AUDIT-C) and negative drinking consequences (B-YAACQ) over and above demographic covariates and CMNI-29 masculine norms, explicitly naming both Perrotte et al. (2020) and Zamboanga et al. (2023) as the prior MDNM studies being replicated and directly comparing the CFA factor structure, positive excess associations, and null control associations against Zamboanga et al. (2023) in the Discussion (lines 634-642, 732-740). The References section (lines 1075-1078) provides the complete citation and DOI: Zamboanga BL, Perrotte JK, Newins AR, Martin JL, Ford K, Wyrick DL, & Milroy JJ (2023), 'Masculine drinking norms and alcohol use in a national sample of NCAA male student-athletes.', Psychology of Men & Masculinities, 24(3), 261-268, DOI 10.1037/men0000436. The only shipped row for this work is input_row_index 2484 (Perrotte, Zamboanga, & Kearns, 2020, DOI 10.1037/men0000252, matched to sibling blind target 0), which is a distinct prospective study of Latino college men; Zamboanga et al. (2023) is a separate empirical study of NCAA male student-athletes and is genuinely omitted from the shipped dataset.

decisions.reason: The available source text (Fox, Gould, Davies, & Owen, 1999, 'Patients’ experiences of having an underwater seal chest drain: a replication study') contains only the title, author list, and abstract. While the abstract explicitly states that a previous single small-scale study on chest drain patients' information needs and pain control was empirically replicated in a second hospital two years later with broadly similar findings, the abstract gives no author names, year, title, or DOI for that prior study. Without full text or references in the primary source, it cannot be verified from source evidence alone whether the replicated study is the shipped row 2433 (Owen & Gould, 1997, 'Underwater seal chest drains: the patient's experience', DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2702.1997.tb00307.x) or a different unshipped report.
